afni.description: AFNI (Analysis of Functional NeuroImages) is a leading software suite of C, Python, R programs and shell scripts primarily developed for the analysis and display of anatomical and functional MRI (FMRI) data. It is freely available (both in source code and in precompiled binaries) for research purposes. The software is made to run on virtually any Unix system with X11 and Motif displays. aidamri.description: The Atlas-based Processing Pipeline for functional and structural MRI data (AIDAmri) was developed for automated processing of mouse brain MRI. AIDAmri works with T2-weighted MRI (T2w), diffusion weighted MRI or diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and resting-state functional MRI (fMRI). The Allen Mouse Brain Reference Atlas (ARA, CCF v3) is registered on each of these MRI data sets and is used to analyse regions of interest. Furthermore, the regions of the ARA are used as seed-points for the connectivity and activity matrices. The lib User-defined ROIs and masks can be generated separately and used for analysis, e.g. stroke lesion masks and peri-infarct regions.

arfimapping.description: OpenRecon Bloch-Siegert B1 mapping from reconstructed magnitude and phase image messages. The runtime implements the workflow from `Read_7T_all_rev_openRecon.m`: detects 1Tx versus 8Tx from the frame count, uses the revised four-echo calculation, dedicated transmit-phase frames, and pre/post reference frames, builds an optional QC magnitude mask, converts phase counts to radians, corrects the scanner DICOM BSp polarity, computes BSp, measured B1, phase, and B0, then sends selected maps as explicit MRD volume images. Default outputs are B1, BSp, Tx phase, and B0 maps. Enable `sendmask` to also return the computed QC mask. The default phase scaling is the MATLAB DICOM conversion `phase * 2*pi/4096 - pi`. Every complete, nonconstant 3D output volume is mapped to scanner pixels spanning `0..4095`; DICOM rescaling and image comments record the inverse mapping back to physical units. B1 is reported in uT, BSp and Tx phase in degrees, B0 in Hz, and the mask as binary. Small negative BSp values are retained in the phase output and clamped only in the separate nonnegative copy used for the B1 square-root calculation. OpenRecon runtime notes: `recipes/blochsiegertb1mapping/OpenReconREADME.md`. Build and validate:

arfirecon.description: OpenRecon ARFI magnitude and phase reconstruction. Every magnitude and phase frame is returned as a multi-slice 2D series with source geometry and slice positions preserved. Single Freq divides one-based frames into sequential groups of `ARFI Block Length`. Odd groups form the noFUS set and even groups form the withFUS set. Multiple Freq uses `myTemp = floor((sqrt(floor((frame_number-1)/2)*8+1)+1)/2)` and assigns a frame to withFUS when `frame_number > myTemp * myTemp`. The runtime forms complex data as `magnitude * exp(i * phase)`, averages the withFUS and noFUS sets independently, and outputs `angle(withFUS_average * conj(noFUS_average))` as `<source> ARFI phase`. Magnitude and wrapped phase frames are also returned in `<source> Magnitude` and `<source> Phase` series. When `Send Phase Standard Deviation` is enabled, every complex frame is multiplied by the conjugate of its set's complex mean. The sample standard deviation of the residual phase is output separately as `<source> withFUS phase standard deviation` and `<source> noFUS phase standard deviation`. A one-frame set produces zero. Phase outputs are converted to degrees. Nonconstant volumes use DICOM pixels `0..4095`, with `RescaleSlope` and `RescaleIntercept` recording the mapping back to physical values. Outputs use `Keep_image_geometry = 1` and are sent as one 2D image per slice with the matching source position. `ARFI Schemes` defaults to Single Freq, `ARFI Block Length` defaults to 25, and `Send Phase Standard Deviation` defaults to disabled. The runtime does not calculate B1, Bloch-Siegert phase, B0, or a mask. OpenRecon runtime notes: `recipes/arfirecon/OpenReconREADME.md`. Build and validate:

aslprep.description: This pipeline is developed by the Satterthwaite lab at the University of Pennysilvania for use at the The Lifespan Informatics and Neuroimaging Center at the University of Pennylvannia, as well as for open-source software distribution. ASLPrep is a Arterial Spin Labeling (ASL) data preprocessing and Cerebral Blood FLow (CBF) computation pipeline that is designed to provide an easily accessible, state-of-the-art interface that is robust to variations in scan acquisition protocols and that requires minimal user input, while providing easily interpretable and comprehensive error and output reporting. It performs basic processing steps (coregistration, normalization, unwarping, noise component extraction, segmentation, skullstripping etc.), CBF computation, denoising CBF, CBF partial volume correction and providing outputs that can be easily submitted to a variety of group level analyses, including task-based or resting-state CBF, graph theory measures, surface or volume-based statistics, etc. The input dataset is required to be in valid BIDS format, and it must include at least one T1w structural image.

bart.description: The Berkeley Advanced Reconstruction Toolbox (BART) is a free and open-source image-reconstruction framework for Computational Magnetic Resonance Imaging. It consists of a programming library and a toolbox of command-line programs. The library provides common operations on multi-dimensional arrays, Fourier and wavelet transforms, as well as generic implementations of iterative optimization algorithms. The command-line tools provide direct access to basic operations on multi-dimensional arrays as well as efficient implementations of many calibration and reconstruction algorithms for parallel imaging and compressed sensing.

blochsiegertb1mapping.description: OpenRecon Bloch-Siegert B1 mapping from reconstructed magnitude and phase image messages. The runtime implements the workflow from `Read_7T_all_rev_openRecon.m`: detects 1Tx versus 8Tx from the frame count, uses the revised four-echo calculation, dedicated transmit-phase frames, and pre/post reference frames, builds phase and magnitude masks, converts phase counts to radians, corrects the scanner DICOM BSp polarity, computes BSp, measured B1, phase, and B0, then sends selected maps as explicit MRD volume images. B1 and B0 maps are always returned. BSp and Tx phase remain configurable, and the computed masks are never returned. When Apply Mask is enabled, the MATLAB-derived magnitude mask is applied to every returned map. Mask holes are filled slice by slice and then across the 3D volume. BS phase/B1 and B0 are filtered with a polynomial fit (order 20 for 1Tx, order 10 for 8Tx) and Gaussian sigma 0.5; Apply Filter changes BS phase from untrusted-only replacement to whole-volume replacement. The default phase scaling is the MATLAB DICOM conversion `phase * 2*pi/4096 - pi`. Every complete, nonconstant 3D output volume is mapped to scanner pixels spanning `0..4095`; DICOM rescaling and image comments record the inverse mapping back to physical units. B1 is reported in uT, BSp and Tx phase in degrees, and B0 in Hz. For 1Tx, a reference-amplitude map in V is also returned using `11.74 * ABS_Tx_Ref_Amp / B1`. Processing-information histogram images are generated for masked B1 (one per Tx channel) and masked B0; they use uT and Hz source units respectively. Small negative BSp values are retained in the phase output and clamped only in the separate nonnegative copy used for the B1 square-root calculation. brats.description: BraTS gives a single interface over the winning algorithms from the BraTS challenges: adult and paediatric glioma, meningioma, brain metastasis and sub-Saharan Africa segmentation, plus inpainting and missing-MRI synthesis. Part of the BrainLesion Suite (BLS): https://github.com/BrainLesion ### Read this first: no algorithms are bundled This container is an orchestrator. It contains no model and no weights. Each of the 66 algorithms is a separate container published by its authors, between roughly 4 GB and over 30 GB compressed -- and the cached sandbox is larger still: a 4 GB pull unpacks to about 8 GB on disk, a 9 GB pull to about 14 GB. You pull the ones you want, once. ### GPU or CPU? Most algorithms need a GPU: only 16 of the 66 are CPU-compatible, and 7 of the 8 task defaults are GPU-only, so on a CPU node `brats -t <task>` without `-a` fails for every task except `africa`. The `adult-glioma-pre`, `pediatric` and `goat` tasks have no CPU-compatible algorithm at all. `brats-algorithms` marks each algorithm `CPU-OK` or `GPU-only`, and `brats-algorithms --cpu-only` lists just the ones a CPU node can run; pick one with `-a`. Incompatibility is also detected before anything is downloaded. CPU runtimes differ by more than two orders of magnitude between algorithms, from about a minute to several hours per subject. `brats-algorithms` shows the estimate where upstream records one; size Slurm walltimes accordingly. **Step 1 -- point the cache at persistent storage.** The cache lives under `$TMPDIR` inside the container; anything in `/tmp` is lost with the session. The module wrapper runs this container with `--cleanenv`, which strips a plain `TMPDIR` export, so use the prefixed form, which survives it:

chimera-brainparcellation.description: CHIMERA combines atlases into custom brain parcellations. This is connectomicslab's brain-parcellation tool, distinct from UCSF Chimera. dafne.description: Dafne is a program for the segmentation of medical images, specifically MR images, that includes advanced deep learning models for an automatic segmentation. The user has the option of refining the automated results, and the software will learn from the improvements and modify its internal models accordingly. In order to continuously improve the performance, the deep learning modules are stored in a central server location. Dafne uses incremental learning and federated learning to continuously adapt the models to the need of our users. This means that when you perform a segmentation, initially it will not be perfect. You will then have the chance to refine it. When you are satisfied with your dataset, you will export your ROI masks (see below). During this export procedure, the software automatically learns from your refined segmentation and sends the updated model back to our servers. This is why the export procedure takes some time. We will automatically integrate your updated model with the models of our other users, so you will always receive the most accurate predictor. You can also manually perform the incremental learning from the Tools menu (see below)

elastix.description: a toolbox for rigid and nonrigid registration of images. elastix is open source software, based on the well-known Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit (ITK). The software consists of a collection of algorithms that are commonly used to perform (medical) image registration: the task of finding a spatial transformation, mapping one image (the fixed image) to another (the moving image), by optimizing relevant image similarity metrics. The modular design of elastix allows the user to quickly configure, test, and compare different registration methods for a specific application. A command-line interface enables automated processing of large numbers of data sets, by means of scripting. Nowadays elastix is accompanied by ITKElastix making it available in Python (on Pypi) and by SimpleElastix, making it available in languages like C++, Python, Java, R, Ruby, C# and Lua.

fastcsr.description: Reconstructing cortical surfaces from structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a prerequisite for surface-based functional and anatomical image analyses. Conventional algorithms for cortical surface construction are computationally inefficient and typically take several hours for each subject, causing a bottleneck in applications when fast turnaround time is needed. To address this challenge, here we proposed a fast cortical surface reconstruction (FastCSR) pipeline based on deep machine learning.

fastsurfer.description:
FastSurfer provides a fully compatible FreeSurfer alternative for volumetric analysis (within minutes) and surface-based thickness analysis (within only around 1h run time). FastSurfer is transitioning to sub-millimeter resolution support throughout the pipeline.

The FastSurfer pipeline consists of two main parts for segmentation and surface reconstruction.

the segmentation sub-pipeline (seg) employs advanced deep learning networks for fast, accurate segmentation and volumetric calculation of the whole brain and selected substructures.

the surface sub-pipeline (recon-surf) reconstructs cortical surfaces, maps cortical labels and performs a traditional point-wise and ROI thickness analysis.

FastSurfer also has a dedicated pipeline to quantify longitudinal changes in T1-weighted MRI. FastSurfer’s longitudinal pipeline outperforms independent (cross-sectional) processing of individual MRIs across time in both FastSurfer and FreeSurfer, as well as even the longitudinal pipeline in FreeSurfer.

frisgo.description: OpenRecon image-to-image Fuzzy Ripple correction for dual-polarity (3D-)EPI BOLD time series, using `LN2_FRISGO -tshift` from LayNii 2.10.0. The OpenRecon module collects every reconstructed image of the run, arranges them by slice position and repetition into a 4D NIfTI, runs `LN2_FRISGO -input timeseries.nii -tshift` and returns: - the original time series on `image_series_index = 100` (`sendoriginal`) - the FRISGO-corrected time series `<source>-frisgo` on `image_series_index = 101` (`sendfrisgo`) Both outputs keep the source 2D geometry, slice and repetition counters with `Keep_image_geometry = 1`. Corrected values are rounded to the source pixel type, so negative values clip to 0 for unsigned scanner images. The GUI selects Spline (default), Simple, Low-pass or Run-wise. Spline requires 4 repetitions; other modes require 2. Low-pass also requires at least 100 spatial voxels. Its Gaussian window defaults to 40 TRs and accepts 0.1 to 1000000 TRs, including fractional values. The window applies only to Low-pass. Invalid selections skip correction and preserve requested originals. Nondefault corrected series identify the algorithm in their suffix and processing history. Incomplete runs, repetition gaps and duplicate nonconstant counters skip correction for that source group while preserving requested originals. Echo, phase, set and average counters define independent time series. Long outputs split into new series before the 16-bit image index overflows. Simulate the OpenRecon round trip with a 4D NIfTI:

gigaconnectome.description: Functional connectivity is a common approach in analysing resting state fMRI data. The Python tool Nilearn provides utilities to extract and denoise time-series on a parcellation. Nilearn also has methods to compute functional connectivity. While Nilearn provides useful methods to generate connectomes, there is no standalone one stop solution to generate connectomes from fMRIPrep outputs. giga-connectome (a BIDS-app!) combines Nilearn and TemplateFlow to denoise the data, generate timeseries, and most critically giga-connectome generates functional connectomes directly from fMRIPrep outputs. The workflow comes with several built-in denoising strategies and there are several choices of atlases (MIST, Schaefer 7 networks, DiFuMo, Harvard-Oxford). Users can customise their own strategies and atlases using the configuration json files.

kul-vbg.description: KUL_VBG performs virtual brain grafting for MRI with large lesions. The scripts, templates, atlases and label tables are installed together in /opt/kul-vbg. UPSTREAM_COMMIT records the exact source revision. Run `KUL_VBG.sh -h`. Upstream returns exit code 1 after printing help. The initial route uses ANTs extraction with `-B 2` and FreeSurfer with `-P 1`: `KUL_VBG.sh -S subject -a /data/T1w.nii.gz -l /data/lesion.nii.gz -z T1 -B 2 -P 1 -m /output/intermediate -o /output/results`. The lesion mask must occupy the same space as the T1 image. Run from a writable working directory and mount writable intermediate/output paths. Supply your own FreeSurfer license at a mounted path and set FS_LICENSE to it. The workflow checks the license even when parcellation is not selected. The image provides ANTs 2.4.3, FSL 6.0.7.18, MRtrix 3.0.8 and FreeSurfer 7.4.1. HD-BET and FastSurfer routes are not packaged. Use -B 2 and -P 1 to keep the workflow within this image rather than upstream's optional nested Docker paths. Only KUL_VBG.sh is exported as a supported module command. The retained KUL_VBG_cook_template.sh and KUL_synth_pats_4VBG.sh source scripts under /opt/kul-vbg are unsupported upstream examples. They require HD-BET and changes to hardcoded input and atlas paths before use. The container label follows the script's recorded software version, 0.61_23112021_beta, with numeric padding. Commit updates retain that software label and use the build date. Licensed autorecon1 preprocessing and ANTs lesion filling with -B 2 have been exercised on a public IXI T1 with a synthetic lesion. The filled image preserves native geometry and contains finite intensities throughout the lesion. lesionquantificationtoolkit.description:
LQT is an R implementation of the lesion quantification toolkit, based on the paper “Lesion Quantification Toolkit: A MATLAB software tool for estimating grey matter damage and white matter disconnections in patients with focal brain lesions” by Griffis et al. The LQT is “a publicly available software package for quantifying the structural impacts of focal brain lesions. It uses atlas-based approaches to estimate parcel-level grey matter lesion loads and multiple measures of white matter disconnection severity that include tract-level disconnection measures, voxel-wise disconnection maps, and parcel-wise disconnection matrices. The toolkit also estimates lesion-induced increases in the lengths of the shortest structural paths between parcel pairs, which provide information about changes in higher-order structural network topology.”

The R package creates data structures necessary for applying the methods directly to MNI-registered lesion maps from either a single patient or a full study. The package then allows the user to create figures for visualization and summary, and to compile analysis-ready datasets for research.

modsort.description: modsort sorts, identifies and tags MR sequences through a drag-and-drop desktop interface, then copies and renames the files into the structure you choose. It is a graphical tool: there is no batch or command line mode. Part of the BrainLesion Suite (BLS): https://github.com/BrainLesion ### Input format modsort is **NIfTI only**. Its drop targets are BraTS-style modality tags -- `_t1.nii.gz`, `_t1c.nii.gz`, `_t2.nii.gz`, `_fla.nii.gz`, plus `swi`, `dwi`, `adc` and `rcbv`. openreconi2iexample.description: Minimal OpenRecon image-to-image reference. Receives reconstructed MRD image messages and sends outputs according to the enabled output options. The scanner label defaults enable original pass-through, inversion, and segmentation. Inversion is also the runtime default when no parameter payload is provided. Enable `sendoriginal` to pass the original 2D image stream through on `image_series_index = 100`. Inverted magnitude images are returned as `<source>-inverted` on `image_series_index = 99`; disable `invert` to omit them. Enable `segment` to extract the brightest foreground object and send `<source>-segment` outputs starting on `image_series_index = 101`. Segment output handling is controlled by `segmentheadergeometry`: `explicit_volume_derived_header` sends segmentation as an explicit derived volume, `3d_series_segment_header` sends 3D source-geometry masks with segmentation header identity, `2d_segment_header` sends 2D source-geometry masks with segmentation header identity, `2d_segment_header_originals` sends the same masks without scanner postprocessing child-role metadata, `2d_derived_image_header` sends 2D source-geometry masks with derived image header identity, and `2d_source_image_header` sends 2D source-geometry masks with source image header identity. When originals and segments are both enabled, originals are sent first and segment outputs are sent after them. Multi-contrast inputs with repeated slice positions are split into one segmentation output per source volume group. Enable `segmentationcolormap` with `segment` to add `MicroDeltaHotMetal.pal` LUT metadata to segmentation outputs. Enable `upsampled` to send one double-slice-count `<source>-upsampled` volume on `image_series_index = 102`. Enable `sendreformatsagittal` or `sendreformatcoronal` to send explicit sagittal/coronal 3D reformat volumes of the segment data starting on `image_series_index = 121`. Enable `sendcomputedmip` to send one `<source>-mip` maximum intensity projection image on `image_series_index = 103`. Enable `sendmetrics` to send segmented-region volume in image comments and a `<source>-metrics` DICOM image table on `image_series_index = 120`. The metrics table is sent as a standalone explicit derived output so scanner inline postprocessing does not attach to it. The rendered pixels are pre-oriented for scanner display and use standalone identity geometry instead of inheriting scan orientation. Original copies are normally sent first as source-native 2D images with `Keep_image_geometry = 1`. The pass-through keeps the source protocol, sequence, image-type, MiniHead, and slice metadata as intact as possible while assigning new returned-series UIDs. Returned originals use a one-based per-series `image_index`. Meta and MiniHead storage counters are restamped from the returned stream so `NumberInSeries`, `ChronSliceNo`, and `SliceNo` remain consistent with the MRD header; valid source partition counters are preserved for multi-partition inputs such as wholebody Dixon. If a source group cannot be sent safely as a 2D stream, the job fails before send rather than packing the originals, because scanner MIP/MPR postprocessing depends on the original stream. When `sendoriginal` is paired with `segmentheadergeometry = explicit_volume_derived_header`, the returned originals are sorted by projected physical slice position so their frame order matches the returned explicit segment volume. With `segmentheadergeometry = explicit_volume_derived_header`, segmentation outputs are sent as one explicit derived volume per source group with `Keep_image_geometry = 0`, `DataRole = Image`, and `SegmentExplicitVolume = 1`. These outputs are batched separately from originals. With `segmentheadergeometry = 3d_series_segment_header`, segmentation outputs are sent as one returned 3D-derived series per source group with one MRD image per source slice. The slices use `Keep_image_geometry = 1`, `DataRole = Segmentation`, `SegmentSourceGeometry = 1`, `SegmentOutputGeometry = 3d`, unique returned `slice` / `image_index` counters, source physical positions, and restamped Meta and MiniHead storage fields. With `segmentheadergeometry = 2d_segment_header`, masks keep source physical geometry, use `Keep_image_geometry = 1`, `DataRole = Segmentation`, `SegmentSourceGeometry = 1`, and the explicit segmentation `ImageType`. With `segmentheadergeometry = 2d_segment_header_originals`, masks use the same source-geometry segmentation header identity, but do not set `SegmentPostProcessingChildRole` or restamp `ExamDataRole` on the segment stream so scanner postprocessing can remain on the original stream. With `segmentheadergeometry = 2d_derived_image_header`, masks use the same source-geometry 2D header path but keep `DataRole = Image` and use a derived segment `ImageType`. With `segmentheadergeometry = 2d_source_image_header`, masks use the same source-geometry 2D header path but keep `DataRole = Image` and source `ImageType`, `DicomImageType`, and `ImageTypeValue4` identity. Segment reformats are packed explicit 3D volumes with centered slab geometry, `Keep_image_geometry = 0`, no `IceMiniHead`, `image_index = 1`, `slice = 0`, and matching `slice_count`, `NumberOfSlices`, and `ImagesInAcquisition`. When originals and segments are both enabled, segment outputs are sent after original outputs in a separate MRD image message. Returned outputs strip scanner `ImageTypeValue3` metadata and `IceMiniHead` `ImageTypeValue3` entries because some sequences reject that protocol field during OpenRecon conversion. Original pass-through preserves Dixon subtype identity. 2D source-image-header mask outputs preserve source identity, including Dixon subtype tokens. OpenRecon runtime notes and scanner option-combination tables: `recipes/openreconi2iexample/OpenReconREADME.md`. Scanner logs include an `openreconi2iexample runtime version=...` marker, `OPENRECONI2I_POSTPROCESSING target=...`, the independent segment controls in the configured-output line, and one `OPENRECONI2I_BATCH ...` marker before every MRD image send. palm.description: PALM \u2014 Permutation Analysis of Linear Models \u2014 is a tool that allows inference using permutation methods, offering a number of features not available in other analysis software. These features currently include: Ability to work with volumetric and surface-based formats, including facewise data, as well as with non-imaging data; A range of various regression and permutation strategies; Statistics that are robust to heteroscedasticity; Shuffling of sets of observations, to allow, for instance, the analysis of certain designs with repeated measurements, with no missing data; Shuffling of observations with complex, tree-like covariance structure (such as for the Human Connectome Project); Permutation with sign-flipping (wild bootstrap); Modified Non-Parametric Combination (NPC) for joint inference over multiple modalities, or multiple contrasts, or both together, with various combining functions available; Classical multivariate statistics (MANOVA, MANCOVA) for joint inference over multiple modalities, assessed through robust permutation methods, and also parametrically when such approximations exist; Correction over multiple contrasts, multiple modalities, for images with or without the same size or geometry, including non-imaging data, controlling the FWER or FDR; Various acceleration methods based on the test statistics and their distributions.
palm.citation:
The main reference for PALM is the same as for randomise:

* Winkler AM, Ridgway GR, Webster MA, Smith SM, Nichols TE. Permutation inference for the general linear model. NeuroImage, 2014;92:381-397 (Open Access)

For correction across contrasts (option -corrcon), the most detailed reference is:

* Alberton BAV, Nichols TE, Gamba HR, Winkler AM. Multiple testing correction over contrasts for brain imaging. Neuroimage. 2020 Mar 19:116760. (Open Access)

For Non-Parametric Combination (NPC; options -npc, -npcmod and -npccon), classical multivariate tests (MANOVA, MANCOVA; option -mv) assessed with permutations, and for correction over contrasts and/or modalities (options -corrcon and -corrmod), the reference is:

* Winkler AM, Webster MA, Brooks JC, Tracey I, Smith SM, Nichols TE. Non-Parametric Combination and related permutation tests for neuroimaging. Hum Brain Map. 2016 Apr;37(4):1486-511. (Open Access)

For the multi-level exchangeability blocks (options -eb, -vg, and for HCP data), the reference is:

* Winkler AM, Webster MA, Vidaurre D, Nichols TE, Smith SM. Multi-level block permutation. Neuroimage. 2015;123:253-68. (Open Access)

* Winkler AM, Ridgway GR, Douaud G, Nichols TE, Smith SM. Faster permutation inference in brain imaging. Neuroimage. 2016 Jun 7;141:502-516. (Open Access)

For additional theory of permutation tests in neuroimaging, please see and cite:

* Nichols TE, Holmes AP. Nonparametric permutation tests for functional neuroimaging: a primer with examples. Hum Brain Map. 2002 Jan;15(1):1-25.

quantiphyse.description: Quantiphyse is a volumetric medical-image viewer and analysis application. This recipe includes its ASL and Fabber plugins, OXASL Python extensions, and a minimal FSL backend with ASL models, image utilities, BET and FLIRT. Start the graphical application with quantiphyse. A display is required. Use quantiphyse-python for Python scripts in the same environment. Headless batch scripts run with quantiphyse --batch /path/to/script.yaml. Quantiphyse: 0.9.10 ASL plugin: 0.9.3.post4 Fabber plugin: 0.9.2 The smoke test checks plugin discovery, label/control subtraction, a small ASL model fit and the GUI's ASL controls under Xvfb. These checks do not validate clinical accuracy. This is not a complete FSL installation: standard space templates, FAST, FNIRT and MCFLIRT are not bundled. OXASL workflows that require those tools need a full FSL environment and separate validation. The minimal backend uses an explicit artifact/checksum lock. Refresh the whole lock together when changing backend versions, then repeat model and GUI tests. Dependency source checks verify the pinned FSL artifacts. OXASL_ENABLE is not included: its Oxford academic licence forbids redistribution, and oxasl treats it as optional. oxasl_mp is built from the Apache-2.0 upstream commit because the only PyPI release (2.0.1) predates the relicensing and lacks the run() entrypoint that oxasl 0.2.3 calls. The bundled pyfab 0.3.6 has a Python 3.10 compatibility patch that moves Sequence lookups to collections.abc. The smoke test exercises the model parameter-evaluation path that requires it. Quantiphyse and its plugins are Apache-2.0. FSL components have separate terms, including restrictions on commercial use. It enhances traditional tractometry, which often misses valuable information due to its reliance on bare summary statistics and scalar values. scipion.description: Scipion is an image processing framework for cryo-electron microscopy. It integrates many cryo-EM packages into reproducible, traceable workflows that you build and run from a graphical project manager or from Python. This container installs Scipion 3.9.0 with scipion-installer 3.0.0 into a conda environment (Python 3.10.22) under /opt/scipion: - scipion-app 3.9.0 - scipion-pyworkflow 3.12.0 - scipion-em (pwem) 3.11.1 Run `scipion3` to open the project manager (Tk GUI). Other useful commands: - `scipion3 version` prints the installed package versions - `scipion3 protocols` lists the available protocols - `scipion3 printenv` shows the effective configuration - `scipion3 python script.py` runs a script with pyworkflow and pwem importable - `scipion3 tests --help` lists the built-in test runner options Projects are stored in `SCIPION_USER_DATA`, which defaults to `~/ScipionUserData`. If your home directory is not writable, the launcher falls back to `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/ScipionUserData-<uid>` and prints a warning. Set `SCIPION_USER_DATA` to a persistent directory to keep projects in that case. Test datasets downloaded by `scipion3 testdata` go to `$SCIPION_USER_DATA/data/tests` unless `SCIPION_TESTS` is set. A personal configuration file at `~/.config/scipion/scipion.conf`, or the file named by `SCIPION_LOCAL_CONFIG`, overrides the defaults. The container provides the Scipion core and the protocols bundled with pwem (data import, subsets, masks and others). It does not include plugins that wrap external programs (Xmipp, RELION, CTFFIND, MotionCor2, ...). The installation is read-only, so `scipion3 installp` and the plugin manager cannot add plugins at runtime. Use the dedicated Neurodesk containers for those programs. synthseg.description: SynthSeg is a contrast- and resolution-agnostic brain MRI segmentation tool. It is trained on synthetic data generated with domain randomisation, so a single network segments scans of any contrast and resolution without retraining or preprocessing. Pass `--keepgeom` to resample the label map back onto the input grid.
